claim: Transcriptional pausing underlies regulation of cellular RNA biogenesis.
source: Transcriptional pausing underlies regulation of cellular RNA biogenesis.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature and the regulatory mechanisms described in the paper.

claim: A consensus pause sequence acts on RNA polymerases (RNAPs) from bacteria to mammals.
source: A consensus pause sequence that acts on RNA polymerases (RNAPs) from bacteria to mammals halts RNAP in an elemental paused state from which longer-lived pauses can arise.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work on consensus pause sequences (Larson et al., 2014) and is a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The consensus pause sequence halts RNAP in an elemental paused state from which longer-lived pauses can arise.
source: A consensus pause sequence that acts on RNA polymerases (RNAPs) from bacteria to mammals halts RNAP in an elemental paused state from which longer-lived pauses can arise.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by the experimental data and kinetic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structural foundations of pauses prolonged by backtracking or nascent RNA hairpins are recognized.
source: Although the structural foundations of pauses prolonged by backtracking or nascent RNA hairpins are recognized, the fundamental mechanism of the elemental pause is less well-defined.
evidence: This statement refers to established knowledge in the field, as indicated by the contrast with the less well-defined elemental pause mechanism.

claim: The fundamental mechanism of the elemental pause is less well-defined.
source: Although the structural foundations of pauses prolonged by backtracking or nascent RNA hairpins are recognized, the fundamental mechanism of the elemental pause is less well-defined.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The elemental pause signal is multipartite.
source: Here we report a mechanistic dissection that establishes the elemental pause signal (i) is multipartite
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by mutational analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: The elemental pause signal causes a modest conformational shift that puts γ-proteobacterial RNAP in an off-pathway state.
source: Here we report a mechanistic dissection that establishes the elemental pause signal (i) is multipartite; (ii) causes a modest conformational shift that puts γ-proteobacterial RNAP in an off-pathway state in which template base loading but not RNA translocation is inhibited
evidence: This finding is supported by kinetic modeling, fluorescence assays, and structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the elemental pause state, template base loading but not RNA translocation is inhibited.
source: Here we report a mechanistic dissection that establishes the elemental pause signal (i) is multipartite; (ii) causes a modest conformational shift that puts γ-proteobacterial RNAP in an off-pathway state in which template base loading but not RNA translocation is inhibited
evidence: This is supported by the 6-MI fluorescence translocation assays shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The elemental pause allows RNAP to enter pretranslocated and one-base-pair backtracked states easily.
source: Here we report a mechanistic dissection that establishes the elemental pause signal (i) is multipartite; (ii) causes a modest conformational shift that puts γ-proteobacterial RNAP in an off-pathway state in which template base loading but not RNA translocation is inhibited; and (iii) allows RNAP to enter pretranslocated and one-base-pair backtracked states easily even though the half-translocated state observed in paused cryo-EM structures rate-limits pause escape.
evidence: This is supported by GreA/B cleavage assays and intrinsic cleavage data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The half-translocated state observed in paused cryo-EM structures rate-limits pause escape.
source: Here we report a mechanistic dissection that establishes the elemental pause signal (i) is multipartite; (ii) causes a modest conformational shift that puts γ-proteobacterial RNAP in an off-pathway state in which template base loading but not RNA translocation is inhibited; and (iii) allows RNAP to enter pretranslocated and one-base-pair backtracked states easily even though the half-translocated state observed in paused cryo-EM structures rate-limits pause escape.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data and comparison with cryo-EM structures (Kang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2018; Vos et al., 2018).

claim: During transcription, RNAP at ~30 nt/s or faster is interrupted by ≥1 s pause events every 100–200 bp.
source: During the first step in gene expression, transcription by RNA polymerase (RNAP) at ~30 nt/s or faster is interrupted by ≥1 s pause events every 100–200 bp (Landick, 2006; Larson et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Landick, 2006; Larson et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015).

claim: Pauses underlie diverse mechanisms that regulate gene expression in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: These pauses underlie diverse mechanisms that regulate gene expression in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Figure 1A), including attenuation, antitermination, and promoter-proximal pausing (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Zhang and Landick, 2016; Mayer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Pausing couples transcription to translation in bacteria.
source: Pausing also couples transcription to translation in bacteria or to mRNA splicing in eukaryotes (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017).

claim: Pausing couples transcription to mRNA splicing in eukaryotes.
source: Pausing also couples transcription to translation in bacteria or to mRNA splicing in eukaryotes (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017).

claim: Pausing defines temporal and positional windows for binding of small molecules, regulatory proteins, or regulatory RNAs to the nascent RNA transcript.
source: Pausing also couples transcription to translation in bacteria or to mRNA splicing in eukaryotes (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017); defines temporal and positional windows for binding of small molecules, regulatory proteins, or regulatory RNAs to the nascent RNA transcript (Wickiser et al., 2005; Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Wickiser et al., 2005; Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002).

claim: Pausing mediates nascent RNA folding.
source: Pausing also couples transcription to translation in bacteria or to mRNA splicing in eukaryotes (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017); defines temporal and positional windows for binding of small molecules, regulatory proteins, or regulatory RNAs to the nascent RNA transcript (Wickiser et al., 2005; Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002); mediates nascent RNA folding (Pan et al., 1999; Pan and Sosnick, 2006; Steinert et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Pan et al., 1999; Pan and Sosnick, 2006; Steinert et al., 2017).

claim: Pausing enables termination.
source: Pausing also couples transcription to translation in bacteria or to mRNA splicing in eukaryotes (Landick et al., 1985; Proshkin et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2017); defines temporal and positional windows for binding of small molecules, regulatory proteins, or regulatory RNAs to the nascent RNA transcript (Wickiser et al., 2005; Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002); mediates nascent RNA folding (Pan et al., 1999; Pan and Sosnick, 2006; Steinert et al., 2017); and enables termination (Gusarov and Nudler, 1999; Proudfoot, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Gusarov and Nudler, 1999; Proudfoot, 2016).

claim: RNA folding and interactions of cellular molecules and complexes with the elongating transcription complex modulate pausing.
source: Conversely, RNA folding and the interactions of cellular molecules and complexes (e.g., ribosomes) with the elongating transcription complex (EC) modulate pausing (Toulokhonov et al., 2001; Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002; Yakhnin et al., 2016; Zhang and Landick, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Toulokhonov et al., 2001; Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002; Yakhnin et al., 2016; Zhang and Landick, 2016).

claim: The biophysical mechanism of pausing remains incompletely defined.
source: Despite its crucial role in cellular information processing, the biophysical mechanism of pausing remains incompletely defined.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Most ECs (80% at 37°C) entered a paused state with a lifetime of 5 s.
source: Most ECs (80% at 37°C) entered a paused state (lifetime 5 s; a, Figure 1D,F), whereas some ECs (20%) transcribed past C17 rapidly (lifetime 0.1 s; bypass, Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is directly measured from pause assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Some ECs (20%) transcribed past C17 rapidly with a lifetime of 0.1 s (bypass).
source: Most ECs (80% at 37°C) entered a paused state (lifetime 5 s; a, Figure 1D,F), whereas some ECs (20%) transcribed past C17 rapidly (lifetime 0.1 s; bypass, Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is directly measured from pause assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A minor ePEC population (typically 15%) escaped more slowly with a lifetime of 100 s.
source: Invariably, a minor ePEC population (typically 15%) escaped more slowly (lifetime 100 s; b, Figure 1D,F), requiring double-exponential fitting of the escape rate.
evidence: This is directly measured from pause assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The amounts of slow ePEC and bypass fractions varied among RNAP preparations.
source: This kinetic malleability of ePECs differed from the reproducible kinetics typically observed for hairpin-stabilized pauses like the hisPEC (Toulokhonov et al., 2001; Kyzer et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Halting ECs at C17 for 15 s before GTP addition did not change the 10–20% EC that bypassed the pause.
source: Unlike for the hairpin-stabilized hisPEC (Toulokhonov et al., 2007), halting ECs at C17 for 15 s before GTP addition did not change the 10–20% EC that bypassed the pause (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experiment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The bypass fraction was shifted from ~22% at 100 µM GTP to ~7% at 10 µM GTP.
source: However, the bypass fraction was shifted from ~22% at 100 µM GTP to ~7% at 10 µM GTP, suggesting that GTP can affect a partition between the on-pathway EC and offline elemental pause state.
evidence: This is directly measured from the experiment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GTP can affect a partition between the on-pathway EC and offline elemental pause state.
source: However, the bypass fraction was shifted from ~22% at 100 µM GTP to ~7% at 10 µM GTP, suggesting that GTP can affect a partition between the on-pathway EC and offline elemental pause state.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed GTP concentration-dependent change in bypass fraction.

claim: The unbranched (on-pathway pause) mechanism did not fit the data well, thus favoring a branched mechanism.
source: The unbranched (on-pathway pause) mechanism did not fit the data well, thus favoring a branched mechanism (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is determined by kinetic modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The elemental pause is an offline state that forms in competition with on-pathway nucleotide addition (i.e., in a branched kinetic mechanism).
source: In agreement with most prior ensemble (Kassavetis and Chamberlin, 1981; Kyzer et al., 2007; Toulokhonov et al., 2007; Strobel and Roberts, 2015) and single-molecule (Herbert et al., 2006; Larson et al., 2014; Gabizon et al., 2018) analyses of pausing, we conclude that the elemental pause is an offline state that forms in competition with on-pathway nucleotide addition (i.e., in a branched kinetic mechanism).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by kinetic modeling and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Either or both GreA or GreB had little effect on pause lifetimes.
source: Either or both GreA or GreB had little effect on pause lifetimes, even though 2-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 1 bp backtracked state, appeared much faster than the rate of ePEC escape and 3-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 2 bp backtracked state, were detectable (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,D).
evidence: This is directly measured from the GreA/GreB cleavage assays shown in Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,D.

claim: 2-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 1 bp backtracked state, appeared much faster than the rate of ePEC escape.
source: Either or both GreA or GreB had little effect on pause lifetimes, even though 2-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 1 bp backtracked state, appeared much faster than the rate of ePEC escape and 3-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 2 bp backtracked state, were detectable (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,D).
evidence: This is directly measured from the GreA/GreB cleavage assays shown in Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,D.

claim: 3-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 2 bp backtracked state, were detectable.
source: Either or both GreA or GreB had little effect on pause lifetimes, even though 2-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 1 bp backtracked state, appeared much faster than the rate of ePEC escape and 3-nt cleavage products, indicative of a 2 bp backtracked state, were detectable (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,D).
evidence: This is directly measured from the GreA/GreB cleavage assays shown in Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,D.

claim: The −11rU-dC mismatch virtually eliminated ≥2 nt cleavage indicative of backtracking.
source: The −11rU-dC mismatch virtually eliminated ≥2 nt cleavage indicative of backtracking, reduced 1-nt cleavage indicative of the pretranslocated register, and modestly decreased the slow pause fraction.
evidence: This is directly measured from the intrinsic cleavage assays shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: The −11rU-dC mismatch reduced 1-nt cleavage indicative of the pretranslocated register.
source: The −11rU-dC mismatch virtually eliminated ≥2 nt cleavage indicative of backtracking, reduced 1-nt cleavage indicative of the pretranslocated register, and modestly decreased the slow pause fraction.
evidence: This is directly measured from the intrinsic cleavage assays shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: The −11rU-dC mismatch modestly decreased the slow pause fraction.
source: The −11rU-dC mismatch virtually eliminated ≥2 nt cleavage indicative of backtracking, reduced 1-nt cleavage indicative of the pretranslocated register, and modestly decreased the slow pause fraction.
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The ePEC readily equilibrates among several active-site states, including half-translocated, pretranslocated, and backtracked, with the half-translocated state being the dominant species.
source: A parsimonious explanation is that the ePEC readily equilibrates among several active-site states, including half-translocated, pretranslocated, and backtracked, with the half-translocated state being the dominant species in which the kinetic block to pause escape is manifest.
evidence: This is inferred from the GreA/B and intrinsic cleavage data combined with the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The kinetic block to pause escape is manifest in the half-translocated state.
source: A parsimonious explanation is that the ePEC readily equilibrates among several active-site states, including half-translocated, pretranslocated, and backtracked, with the half-translocated state being the dominant species in which the kinetic block to pause escape is manifest.
evidence: This is inferred from the GreA/B and intrinsic cleavage data combined with the cryo-EM structures and translocation assays.

claim: Alone, the usFJ, dsFJ, and dsDNA mutants reduced PS by a factor of ~5.
source: Alone, the usFJ, dsFJ, and dsDNA mutants reduced PS by a factor of ~5, whereas the Hyb mutant decreased PS by a factor or ~1.4 fold (but see larger effects in Bochkareva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Hyb mutant decreased PS by a factor of ~1.4 fold.
source: Alone, the usFJ, dsFJ, and dsDNA mutants reduced PS by a factor of ~5, whereas the Hyb mutant decreased PS by a factor or ~1.4 fold (but see larger effects in Bochkareva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combinations of mutants produced additive effects on pause strength.
source: Combinations of mutants produced additive effects on pause strength (Figure 2D, magenta brackets; additive effects on an energy barrier are multiplicative in τ or PS; e.g., reduction of PS by factors of 1.4 and 3.7 for the Hyb and dsDNA substitutions predicts a combined reduction by a factor of 5.1 vs. the factor of 5.2 observed).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Additive effects are expected if pause signal components independently affect the same energetic barrier to pause escape.
source: Additive effects are expected if pause signal components independently affect the same energetic barrier to pause escape (e.g., translocation of the template base).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: The lifetimes of the major and minor pause states were highly correlated for the pause-sequence variants.
source: The lifetimes of the major and minor pause states were highly correlated for the pause-sequence variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The slow pause fraction (Eb) was uncorrelated with the major pause escape rate (k-spapp), the major pause fraction (Ea), and the total ePEC fraction (E).
source: In contrast, the slow pause fraction (Eb; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) was uncorrelated with the major pause escape rate (k-spapp), the major pause fraction (Ea), and the total ePEC fraction (E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both the major pause species and the minor, slowly escaping pause species pass through a common barrier for pause escape.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which both the major pause species and the minor, slowly escaping pause species pass through a common barrier for pause escape (e.g., template-base loading).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation of lifetimes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The elemental pause signal is multipartite with significant contributions from sequences in the usFJ, Hyb, dsFJ, and dsDNA to a common kinetic barrier to escape from multiple paused states.
source: We conclude that the elemental pause signal is indeed multipartite with significant contributions from sequences in the usFJ, Hyb, dsFJ, and dsDNA to a common kinetic barrier to escape from multiple paused states.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the mutational analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: For both scaffolds, 2′dCMP gave a 6-MI signal increase comparable to CMP, whereas 3′dCMP reduced the signal increase.
source: For both scaffolds, 2′dCMP gave a 6-MI signal increase comparable to CMP, whereas 3′dCMP reduced the signal increase.
evidence: This is directly measured from the fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Addition of CMP shifts both hybrids toward the posttranslocated register.
source: These results suggested that addition of CMP shifts both hybrids toward the posttranslocated register, although the absolute fluorescence change for the ePEC scaffold was about half that of the control scaffold.
evidence: This is inferred from the 6-MI fluorescence data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: CMP added rapidly (~300 s−1) followed by a rapid (~200 s−1) rise in fluorescence signal indicating translocation on both scaffolds.
source: Rapid-quench and stopped-flow kinetic measurements revealed that CMP added rapidly (~300 s−1) followed by a rapid (~200 s−1) rise in fluorescence signal indicating translocation on both scaffolds.
evidence: This is directly measured from the rapid-quench and stopped-flow experiments shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Subsequent extension to G18 of the ePEC but not the control EC was slow (~0.2 s−1 vs. 40 s−1).
source: In contrast, subsequent extension to G18 of the ePEC but not the control EC was slow (~0.2 s−1 vs. 40 s−1; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is directly measured from the rapid-quench and stopped-flow experiments shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The 6-MI ePEC scaffold produced pause fractions (~85%) and lifetimes similar to the unmodified consensus scaffold.
source: Because the 6-MI and –10 substitutions in the ePEC scaffold could affect pausing, we verified that the 6-MI ePEC scaffold produced pause fractions (~85%) and lifetimes similar to the unmodified consensus scaffold (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: The ePEC hybrid translocates rapidly after CMP addition, resembling the control scaffold.
source: We conclude that the ePEC hybrid translocates rapidly after CMP addition, resembling the control scaffold.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the 6-MI fluorescence data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Most ePECs are not backtracked.
source: These results also confirm that most ePECs are not backtracked, which would not unquench 6-MI (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the 6-MI fluorescence data and the GreA/B cleavage data.

claim: The ePEC, once formed, may easily fluctuate among multiple translocation states.
source: Together the data are fully consistent with a view that the ePEC, once formed, may easily fluctuate among multiple translocation states.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined 6-MI fluorescence, GreA/B cleavage, and intrinsic cleavage data.

claim: For the control scaffold, addition of CMP or 2′dCMP or extension with CTP + GTP to G19 gave a large 6-MI signal indicating translocation after C17 nucleotide addition.
source: For the control scaffold, addition of CMP or 2′dCMP or extension with CTP + GTP to G19 gave a large 6-MI signal indicating translocation after C17 nucleotide addition (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly measured from the fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ePEC scaffold gave minimal 6-MI signal after CMP or 2′dCMP addition compared to extension to G19, which produced a strong 6-MI signal.
source: In contrast, the ePEC scaffold gave minimal 6-MI signal after CMP or 2′dCMP addition (consistent with translocation in only a bypass fraction) compared to extension to G19, which produced a strong 6-MI signal (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly measured from the fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The dsDNA in the ePEC does not translocate.
source: These data confirm that the dsDNA in the ePEC does not translocate.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the 6-MI fluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For the control EC, a clear increase in 6-MI signal was evident as GTP bound in the active site with apparent Kd ≈ 400 µM.
source: For the control EC, a clear increase in 6-MI signal was evident as GTP bound in the active site with apparent Kd ≈ 400 µM (Figure 4D, inset).
evidence: This is directly measured from the GTP titration experiment shown in Figure 4D inset.

claim: Even a high GTP concentration was unable to shift the 3′dC17 ePEC to the post-translocated register.
source: However, even a high GTP concentration was unable to shift the 3′dC17 ePEC to the post-translocated register (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly measured from the GTP titration experiment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The half-translocated state detected in ePEC cryoEM structure also forms in actively transcribing complexes.
source: We conclude that even the weakened elemental pause signal in the dsFJ ePEC assay scaffold prevented dsDNA translocation and thus template-base loading. Taken together, the usFJ and dsFJ 6-MI data confirm that the half-translocated state detected in ePEC cryoEM structure also forms in actively transcribing complexes, and that template-base loading is the relevant barrier to nucleotide addition in the ePEC.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined 6-MI fluorescence data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Template-base loading is the relevant barrier to nucleotide addition in the ePEC.
source: We conclude that even the weakened elemental pause signal in the dsFJ ePEC assay scaffold prevented dsDNA translocation and thus template-base loading. Taken together, the usFJ and dsFJ 6-MI data confirm that the half-translocated state detected in ePEC cryoEM structure also forms in actively transcribing complexes, and that template-base loading is the relevant barrier to nucleotide addition in the ePEC.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined 6-MI fluorescence data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The ePEC did not exhibit constraints on TL conformation compared to control EC.
source: In contrast, the ePEC, whose cryoEM structure is not swiveled, did not exhibit constraints on TL conformation (compare to control EC; Figure 5C,D,E).
evidence: This is directly measured from the CPR crosslinking assays shown in Figure 5C,D,E.

claim: The ePEC accessed the folded TH conformation more readily than did the control EC.
source: If anything, the ePEC accessed the folded TH conformation more readily than did the control EC, consistent with ePEC access to the pretranslocated register (Figure 1J) that is thought to increase TL folding (Malinen et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly measured from the CPR crosslinking assays shown in Figure 5C,D,E and is consistent with prior studies (Malinen et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016).

claim: Inhibition of TL folding does not appear to limit escape from the elemental pause.
source: Thus, inhibition of TL folding does not appear to limit escape from the elemental pause.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the CPR crosslinking data shown in Figure 5.

claim: F937-736 and P937-687 crosslinking in 3′dCMP-ePEC, and therefore TL conformation, were unaffected by high GTP concentration.
source: Consistent with results of the 6-MI dsFJ translocation assay, F937-736 and P937-687 crosslinking in 3′dCMP-ePEC, and therefore TL conformation, were unaffected by high GTP concentration even though the crosslinks formed readily.
evidence: This is directly measured from the CPR crosslinking assays shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: CPR crosslinking in control 3′dCMP-EC exhibited an obvious shift toward TL folding upon ATP binding.
source: In contrast, CPR crosslinking in control 3′dCMP-EC exhibited an obvious shift toward TL folding upon ATP binding (Figure 5E,F; Nayak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly measured from the CPR crosslinking assays shown in Figure 5E,F and is consistent with prior studies (Nayak et al., 2013).

claim: Inability to load the template base inhibits NTP binding in the ePEC.
source: These results are consistent with the ePEC cryoEM structure and translocation assay results, supporting a view that inability to load the template base inhibits NTP binding in the ePEC.
evidence: This is inferred from the CPR crosslinking data shown in Figure 5 combined with the 6-MI translocation data.

claim: The closed-clamp disulfide had minimal effect on the ePEC lifetime.
source: In contrast to suppression of pausing for the hairpin-stabilized hisPEC (Figure 6C; Hein et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2018a), the closed-clamp disulfide had minimal effect on the ePEC lifetime (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Clamp swiveling (or opening) is not required in the ePEC.
source: We conclude that, unlike for hairpin-stabilized pausing and consistent with the cryoEM structure, clamp swiveling (or opening) is not required in the ePEC.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the closed-clamp disulfide data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Formation of the ePEC is accompanied by a loosening of clamp contacts.
source: We conclude that formation of the ePEC is accompanied by a loosening of clamp contacts.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the CTR assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: β′K334A resembled the wild-type enzyme on both consensus and mutant pause scaffolds.
source: Strikingly, β′K334A resembled the wild-type enzyme on both consensus and mutant pause scaffolds, whereas βR542A decreased pausing by a factor of 2 on the consensus pause and dsFJ templates, but significantly more on the usFJ template (13X effect of usFJ vs. 6X for wild-type RNAP; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: βR542A decreased pausing by a factor of 2 on the consensus pause and dsFJ templates.
source: Strikingly, β′K334A resembled the wild-type enzyme on both consensus and mutant pause scaffolds, whereas βR542A decreased pausing by a factor of 2 on the consensus pause and dsFJ templates, but significantly more on the usFJ template (13X effect of usFJ vs. 6X for wild-type RNAP; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: βR542A decreased pausing significantly more on the usFJ template (13X effect of usFJ vs. 6X for wild-type RNAP).
source: Strikingly, β′K334A resembled the wild-type enzyme on both consensus and mutant pause scaffolds, whereas βR542A decreased pausing by a factor of 2 on the consensus pause and dsFJ templates, but significantly more on the usFJ template (13X effect of usFJ vs. 6X for wild-type RNAP; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured from the pause assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: βR542 may help inhibit template dC loading in the ePEC.
source: We conclude that βR542 may help inhibit template dC loading in the ePEC.
evidence: This is inferred from the βR542A mutant data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The elemental pause is a distinct offline state, not an on-pathway elongation intermediate.
source: The elemental pause is a distinct offline state, not an on-pathway elongation intermediate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the kinetic modeling and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The elemental pause involves a modestly rearranged multistate ePEC in which the clamp is loosened and template-base loading is inhibited.
source: Our study uncovered evidence for a modestly rearranged multistate ePEC in which the clamp is loosened and template-base loading is inhibited as well as a slower ePEC state entered by a minor but variable fraction of ECs (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined data from Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: A slower ePEC state is entered by a minor but variable fraction of ECs.
source: Our study uncovered evidence for a modestly rearranged multistate ePEC in which the clamp is loosened and template-base loading is inhibited as well as a slower ePEC state entered by a minor but variable fraction of ECs (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the pause assay data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: When RNAP encounters an elemental pause signal, a modest shift in the mobile modules of RNAP occurs during translocation.
source: To explain how RNAP responds to an elemental pause signal, we propose a multi-state pause mechanism in which pause escape is principally inhibited by inability to load the template base into the active site of RNAP in a half-translocated, off-line intermediate (Figure 8A,B). When RNAP encounters an elemental pause signal, a modest shift in the mobile modules of RNAP that are in contact with RNA and DNA (the clamp, shelf, lid, rudder, switch regions, lobe, protrusion, fork loop 2, and βDloopII) occurs during translocation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined experimental data and comparison with cryo-EM structures.

claim: This shift creates or reinforces an energetic barrier to completion of translocation from a half-translocated state.
source: This shift creates or reinforces an energetic barrier to completion of translocation from a half-translocated state in which the RNA transcript has translocated but the DNA template has not, corresponding to the tilted hybrid intermediate observed in cryo-EM structures (Kang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2018; Vos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined experimental data and comparison with cryo-EM structures (Kang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2018; Vos et al., 2018).

claim: Key contacts preventing DNA translocation involve the lid, rudder, and switch 2.
source: Key contacts preventing DNA translocation involve the lid, rudder, and switch 2 (Kang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2018) as well as apparent H-bonds of R542 in fork loop two to the +1dC–dG bp that may hinder its translocation into the active site (Figures 7A and 8; compare to the conserved Arg in a TthEC, which contacts the backbone phosphate of a template nucleotide loaded into the active site; Vassylyev et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data, structural comparisons, and prior studies (Kang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2018; Vassylyev et al., 2007).

claim: Apparent H-bonds of R542 in fork loop two to the +1dC–dG bp may hinder its translocation into the active site.
source: Key contacts preventing DNA translocation involve the lid, rudder, and switch 2 (Kang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2018) as well as apparent H-bonds of R542 in fork loop two to the +1dC–dG bp that may hinder its translocation into the active site (Figures 7A and 8; compare to the conserved Arg in a TthEC, which contacts the backbone phosphate of a template nucleotide loaded into the active site; Vassylyev et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the βR542A mutant data and structural comparisons.

claim: DNA and RNA in the ePEC can move backwards to form pretranslocated, frayed, 1 bp backtracked, and, much more slowly, ≥2 bp backtracked states.
source: DNA and RNA in the ePEC can move backwards to form pretranslocated, frayed, 1 bp backtracked, and, much more slowly, ≥2 bp backtracked states (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the GreA/B cleavage and intrinsic cleavage data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: At least at the consensus pause, the half-translocated, pretranslocated, and 1 bp backtracked states equilibrate but these equilibria are biased toward the half-translocated state.
source: At least at the consensus pause, the half-translocated, pretranslocated, and 1 bp backtracked states equilibrate but these equilibria are biased toward the half-translocated state.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined 6-MI fluorescence, GreA/B cleavage, and intrinsic cleavage data.

claim: The multistate model of the elemental pause makes the distinction between backtrack pausing and non-backtrack pausing a matter of degree rather than a clear-cut division.
source: The multistate elemental pause model makes the distinction between backtrack pausing and non-backtrack pausing a matter of degree rather than a clear-cut division.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion based on the multistate model proposed in the Discussion.

claim: The existence of multiple elemental pause states affords multiple targets for regulators even when these intermediates are in equilibrium.
source: The multistate model (Figure 8) has important regulatory implications. Just as different regulators can exert distinct effects on the multistep mechanism of transcription initiation by stabilizing or destabilizing different intermediates (Hubin et al., 2017), the existence of multiple elemental pause states affords multiple targets for regulators even when these intermediates are in equilibrium.
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the multistate model, supported by analogy to transcription initiation (Hubin et al., 2017).

claim: ppGpp is known to stimulate pausing.
source: For example, ppGpp is known to stimulate pausing (Kingston et al., 1981) and to promote backtracking (Kamarthapu et al., 2016); ppGpp could stimulate pausing by stabilizing a pretranslocated or backtracked PEC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Kingston et al., 1981; Kamarthapu et al., 2016).

claim: ppGpp is known to promote backtracking.
source: For example, ppGpp is known to stimulate pausing (Kingston et al., 1981) and to promote backtracking (Kamarthapu et al., 2016); ppGpp could stimulate pausing by stabilizing a pretranslocated or backtracked PEC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Kingston et al., 1981; Kamarthapu et al., 2016).

claim: ppGpp could stimulate pausing by stabilizing a pretranslocated or backtracked PEC.
source: For example, ppGpp is known to stimulate pausing (Kingston et al., 1981) and to promote backtracking (Kamarthapu et al., 2016); ppGpp could stimulate pausing by stabilizing a pretranslocated or backtracked PEC.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the multistate model and prior knowledge of ppGpp effects.

claim: The elemental pause signal involves significant contributions from the usFJ, hybrid, dsFJ, and dsDNA.
source: Our results (Figure 2) confirm that, like the hairpin-stabilized hisPEC (Chan et al., 1997), the elemental pause signal is multipartite and involves significant contributions from the usFJ, hybrid, dsFJ, and dsDNA.
evidence: This is directly measured from the mutational analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: Strong evidence of significant contributions by the hybrid and dsDNA exists.
source: Although strong evidence of significant contributions by the hybrid and dsDNA exists (Bochkareva et al., 2012; Larson et al., 2014; Palangat and Landick, 2001; Palangat et al., 2004), some descriptions of pausing focus only on the usFJ and dsFJ (Vvedenskaya et al., 2014; Imashimizu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Bochkareva et al., 2012; Larson et al., 2014; Palangat and Landick, 2001; Palangat et al., 2004).

claim: The inhibitory contributions of the usFJ and dsFJ to hybrid unwinding and NTP binding, respectively, have been known since the earliest studies of pausing.
source: The inhibitory contributions of the usFJ and dsFJ to hybrid unwinding and NTP binding, respectively, have been known since the earliest studies of pausing (Gilbert et al., 1974; Aivazashvili et al., 1981) but alone are inadequate to predict pause strength.
evidence: This is supported by citations to early studies (Gilbert et al., 1974; Aivazashvili et al., 1981).

claim: The usFJ and dsFJ alone are inadequate to predict pause strength.
source: The inhibitory contributions of the usFJ and dsFJ to hybrid unwinding and NTP binding, respectively, have been known since the earliest studies of pausing (Gilbert et al., 1974; Aivazashvili et al., 1981) but alone are inadequate to predict pause strength.
evidence: This is supported by the mutational analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: Quick-freezing reveals the modest sequence signatures of the hybrid and dsDNA in sequence logos and energetic analyses.
source: Quick-freezing reveals the modest sequence signatures of the hybrid and dsDNA in sequence logos and energetic analyses (Figure 2A; Larson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the NET-seq data and analysis from Larson et al., 2014.

claim: Some studies that detected little if any hybrid or dsDNA contribution recovered cells by centrifugation before freezing, which may allow RNAP to escape all but the strongest pause sites.
source: However, some studies that detected little if any hybrid or dsDNA contribution recovered cells by centrifugation before freezing, which may allow RNAP to escape all but the strongest pause sites and thus could over-represent contributions of the usFJ and dsFJ components (Vvedenskaya et al., 2014; Imashimizu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior studies (Vvedenskaya et al., 2014; Imashimizu et al., 2015) based on methodological differences.

claim: The hybrid and dsDNA contact multiple RNAP modules and may principally affect the complex and modest conformational rearrangement into the ePEC state.
source: Finally, the hybrid and dsDNA contact multiple RNAP modules (e.g., rudder, switch 2, clamp, etc.) and may principally affect the complex and modest conformational rearrangement into the ePEC state.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and the mutational analyses.

claim: The elemental pause is a modestly rearranged multistate ePEC in which the clamp is loosened and template-base loading is inhibited.
source: Our study uncovered evidence for a modestly rearranged multistate ePEC in which the clamp is loosened and template-base loading is inhibited as well as a slower ePEC state entered by a minor but variable fraction of ECs (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined data from Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: The multistate model of elemental pausing involves small changes in RNAP conformation and half-translocated, pretranslocated, and multiple 1 bp backtracked states.
source: The multistate model of elemental pausing involving small changes in RNAP conformation and half-translocated, pretranslocated, and multiple 1 bp backtracked states described here will be difficult to test fully using ensemble biochemistry, single-molecule biochemistry, or crystallography.
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed model and a statement about the challenges of testing it.

claim: Time-resolved cryo-EM promises an attractive approach if methods to distinguish intermediates during particle classification can be developed.
source: Time-resolved cryo-EM (Frank, 2017) promises an attractive approach if methods to distinguish intermediates during particle classification can be developed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future experimental approaches, supported by a citation (Frank, 2017).
